e.etymology: In Arabic a girls' name from the verb rana, to gaze, with the sense of eye-catching. In India a boys' name from rana, a Rajput title for a king, the male counterpart of rani.

assoc.t: Rana, refrigerated fresh pasta sold in US supermarkets

e.note: Rana is the Spanish and Italian word for frog.

e.etymology: A respelling of Blaine, a Scottish surname from the Gaelic name Bláán, a diminutive of blá, yellow. Saint Blane was a 6th-century bishop on the Isle of Bute.
A respelling of Cadence, the English word for rhythmic flow in music and speech, from Latin cadere, to fall. Cadence became a girls' name in the early 2000s.
The Italian form of Stephen, from Latin Stephanus and Greek stephanos, crown or wreath. Saint Stephen was the first Christian martyr.
e.note: Italians stress the first syllable (STEH-fah-noh); Americans often stress the second.

e.etymology: From the surname of Saint John Vianney (1786-1859), the French parish priest of Ars. A boys' name in France; in the US it is given mostly to girls, largely in Mexican American families.
From Hebrew Efrayim, fruitful. In Genesis, Ephraim is Joseph's younger son and the ancestor of one of the twelve tribes of Israel. This spelling follows the Hebrew more closely than Ephraim does.
A respelling of Landry, a French surname and medieval saint's name from the Germanic Landric, made up of land, land, and ric, ruler.
The feminine of Robert, from the Germanic elements hrod, fame, and berht, bright. Its American height came in the 1930s and 1940s.
namesakes: Roberta Flack (singer of Killing Me Softly with His Song)

e.etymology: An African American coinage of the later 20th century, possibly a blend of Tyrone with Reese or Maurice. Singer and actor Tyrese Gibson made it widely known in the late 1990s.
namesakes: Tyrese Gibson (R&B singer and Fast & Furious actor)

assoc.t: Tyrese Gibson, singer and actor billed as Tyrese

e.etymology: A respelling of Jalil, from Arabic jalil, great or exalted, one of the names of God in Islam. It rose in the US in the mid-2010s alongside basketball player Jahlil Okafor.
namesakes: Jahlil Okafor (Duke national champion and NBA center)

e.etymology: A name of uncertain origin, usually taken as a form of Niles or Nile. It drew notice in 2015 and 2016 through Nyle DiMarco, the deaf model who won two TV competitions.
namesakes: Nyle DiMarco (deaf model, winner of America's Next Top Model and Dancing with the Stars)

e.etymology: A 2000s American coinage in the family of Aiden, Brayden and Jayden, with the Dr- opening of Drake and Draven.
From Urdu Syeda, from Arabic sayyida, lady, the feminine of sayyid. In South Asia it is an honorific, carried as a first name by women of families that trace descent from the Prophet Muhammad.

e.meaning: smiling child or blessed, beautiful child, depending on the kanji
e.etymology: A Japanese name ending in ko, child. The first part depends on the kanji chosen: often emi written as smile, or e and mi written as blessing and beauty.
From Latin Octavianus, a derivative of the family name Octavius, from octavus, eighth. The future emperor Augustus was known as Octavian after Julius Caesar adopted him.

assoc.t: Rome's first emperor, Augustus, known earlier as Octavian

e.etymology: From Arabic haydar, lion, a title of Ali ibn Abi Talib, the Prophet Muhammad's cousin and son-in-law. Haider is the usual spelling in Pakistan and India.
In Finland, the everyday form of Sakarias, the Biblical Zechariah, from Hebrew for the Lord has remembered. In the US it is given to boys and girls about equally and sits beside Zakari and Jakari.
An English surname from places named in Old English as the white acre, or field. Its use as a first name is recent, helped by the nickname Whit.

e.meaning: chalice (Latin); also short for Calixto, most beautiful
e.etymology: Calix is Latin for cup or chalice. As a name it is also a short form of Calixto or Callixtus, a pope's and saint's name from Greek kallistos, most beautiful, later respelled after the Latin word.
A respelling of Alora, a modern name with no settled origin, close in sound to Elora, Lora and Aurora.
A C spelling of Kalani, from Hawaiian ka lani, the heavens or the sky, also a term for a high chief. Hawaiian has no letter C, so this form is an American respelling.
A one-word spelling of Jo Ann and Joanne, from Latin Joanna and Hebrew Yochanah, God is gracious, the feminine counterpart of John. Its American height came in the 1930s and 1940s.

assoc.t: Joann, fabric and craft store chain that closed in 2025

e.etymology: A Scottish surname from Moray, the region in northeastern Scotland, whose name goes back to Celtic words for sea and settlement. It was a popular American first name in the 1910s and 1920s.
namesakes: Murray Bartlett (Emmy-winning actor in The White Lotus)
Murray Goldberg (the dad on the sitcom The Goldbergs)

e.etymology: From Late Latin Clemens, from clemens, merciful or gentle. Fourteen popes took the name, beginning with Saint Clement I in the first century.
namesakes: Clement Clarke Moore (author of A Visit from St. Nicholas)

e.meaning: tumult; later linked with French triste, sad
e.etymology: A respelling of Tristan, the knight of the Tristan and Iseult legend. The name comes from the Celtic Drust, tied to a word for noise or tumult, and was reshaped in French by triste, sad.
The German, Czech and Scandinavian spelling of Joseph, from Hebrew Yosef, (God) shall add. In Genesis, Joseph is the favored son of Jacob who rises to power in Egypt.
A 1990s feminine form of Taylor, the occupational surname for a tailor. It is most popular in Australia and New Zealand, where it sounds the same as Taylor.
A spelling of Jacey or Jackie, pet forms of Jacqueline, the French feminine of Jacques (James). In Brazil, Jaci is a separate name from the Tupi word for the moon.
namesakes: Jaci Velasquez (Christian and Latin pop singer)

e.etymology: A pet form of Roxanne and Roxana, the Greek form of an Old Persian or Bactrian name akin to Persian roshan, bright. Roxana was the wife of Alexander the Great.

assoc.t: Roxy, Quiksilver's surf and swimwear brand for women
The Roxy, Sunset Strip nightclub in West Hollywood
roxy or roxies, street slang for oxycodone pills

e.etymology: A modern American blend of Ty and Lee, in the pattern of Kylee and Rylee.
A surname meaning son of Lars or Lawrence. In the United States it is mostly an anglicized form of Swedish Larsson and Danish and Norwegian Larsen.
namesakes: Brie Larson (Oscar-winning actress and Captain Marvel star)
Gary Larson (creator of The Far Side comic)

e.etymology: A Persian girls' name from the word for a dream or vision, borrowed from Arabic ru'ya. It is common in Iran, Afghanistan and Azerbaijan.
